deck_zh: 裁决说秋天应当举行选举。执政院说尊重法院，却没有发出选举令。“最后一审”到了这里，还剩下什么？
deck_en: The court orders an election by autumn. The executive says it respects the court, then issues no election order. What does a final judgment amount to now?
body_zh: 裁决出来的第二天，首席执政说：“执政院尊重终审法院。”这句话后面还有一句：在议会终止战时状态以前，执政院不发布选举令。
法院说得并不含糊。停火已经生效，就推迟选举那一款而言，战时状态应算到停火为止；选举最迟在当年秋天举行。六位法官赞成，五位反对。五人的理由也写在案卷里：这不是解释，是改写。执政院同意少数意见，于是多数作出的裁决没有得到执行。
我们仍在目的联合城邦这个假想国家里。这里有十一位终审法官，宪章案件全院审。宪章写着，裁决约束一切机关；却没有写，机关拒不执行时，谁来做。本来该上一年冬天届满的议员和首席执政，仍然留在位置上。
王国州和南湾邦的选举委员会说，可以按原选区筹备。执政院回函：成员单位无权举办国家一级选举。没有办成。次年夏天，撤军协定生效，议会另定日期，选举才在次年秋天举行。晚了一年。
这不是只发生在纸上的分歧。一年里，本来可以通过选举让议员回答的人，少了一次实际发问的机会。“最后”如果还得等败诉的一方同意才算数，那张最后的否决票，就不在法院手里。
## 结的是案，不是以后所有的问
我们当然不能把法院变成一个永远正确的地方。那五位法官可能提出了很有分量的问题，裁决也可能真的错了。但“会错”和“败诉方可以不执行”，不能接成一句话。否则每个机关都可以找到一种解释，把自己变成裁决效力的最后开关。
有效而须执行的裁决，应当执行。不同意，可以公开说明，可以提出修改未来规则的建议。如果认为照办本身会伤害某个人、越过基本边界，也应公开提出，转入不由自己作主的复核，而不是保持沉默、不行动。复核作出之前，裁决仍有效，不能由执行机关借异议自行暂停。紧急状态也不另外赠送这一张否决票。
这里说的是机关职责，不是在替坐在职位上的人决定良心。一个人可以拒绝、可以辞职，他的处境仍要得到保护；但不能因此让整个职位取得使裁决失效的权力。于是最高规则必须留下一条替代落实的路：不待拒绝执行的一方同意，也能启动，启动之后它挡不住。
不必马上想象另建一支军队。这一案缺的是选举令和选举筹办，已经有两个地方的选举委员会愿意办。怎样授权、由谁启动，需要具体设计。替代功能只为落实那一项裁决，不是再造一个不受问的权力中心；它自己也要受检查。设下这项功能，并不担保从此次次都能办成，却不能把拒绝者的点头写成唯一条件。
反过来，执行不容挑选，也不等于法院的职位从此免问。一个案子用同样理由已经审完，可以结束；有新证据、新问题，可以再审；法官受贿、越权、失职，可以追究；规则可以依法修改，作用于以后的案子。公开批评判决，更不需要等到法院先同意。
最后一审结束的是这一件争议，并没有把这些路一并关上。法律需要一个此刻可以照办的决定，人也需要以后仍能纠正错误的机会。两样都要留。
## 七位法官说不，却没有改变拘留
同一年，法院还审了一条紧急拘留令。涉嫌协助敌方者，可以不起诉拘留，每次三十天，可以接着来。七位法官认为它不合宪章，四位认为没有问题。按平常对“多数”的理解，似乎事情已经清楚。
但第十四修正案规定，宣告紧急令不合宪章，得有八票。七票不够。条款继续有效。到那时，已有六百四十人因此被拘留，最长的一位关了一百五十天。
这时不能说“法院已经判拘留令无效，政府不听”。那样把两件不同的事混了。有效程序下的结果，就是没有宣告无效；七位法官的话留成了理由，没有变成能使条款停止适用的决定。
可也不能说“程序如此，事情就到此为止”。门槛改变了什么，在这里看得很清楚：从多数到八票之间的那一段，原本能导向行动的审查，退成了只能说明理由。审查还在，不宜笼统说它已被取消；若门槛高到实际上从来不能影响行动，它又会只剩名字。单凭这一案，还不能下后一个判断。能够确定的是：这一次，七位法官的话没有把人放出来。
新的拘留是新的决定，新材料和新问题可以再带进来；战时特别门槛结束，也是新的条件。法院可以判断某次请求是不是新的，不能一句话宣布此后这一类人永远不再收。对规则提出修改，也不等于推翻已经结束的那一次判决。
## 问法官，也要防止拿提问来换人
让法院接受追问，听起来容易赞同；可追问也可能被用来压法院。那份选举裁决之后，议会弹劾了执笔的首席法官。理由不是判错，而是评议期间曾与请求一方的邦长私下交谈。地点在法学院毕业典礼的休息室，约二十分钟，两位教员在场，说没听到谈案件。法官和邦长也说，谈的是典礼和一位退休法官。
这二十分钟是否失职，案卷还不足以让我们代判。但可以先分清：法官的行为能不能问？能。仅仅因为判决不合多数心意，就能借弹劾把人换掉吗？不能。否则所谓检查法官，就成了不要新证据、不改未来规则、只换一个会作出不同裁决的人。判决内容仍可成为受贿或滥权的证据；不能把“不喜欢结论”本身当成失职。
四位领衔弹劾者中，三位正是先前那一案里代表议会多数出庭的人。这三位应当回避提起和审理这一件弹劾，不必先证明他们心存报复。回避的是具体牵涉的人，不是整个议会；否则只要议会一方曾被审查，法官在那一案里即使受贿也无人能够追究。弹劾理由能否与判决分开，不能只由发动弹劾的一方决定。
这次还有自动停职。弹劾一提出，首席法官就离开了在审案件三个月，法院少了一人。后来定罪票没达到门槛，他复职了。我们不知道他如果在场会怎样投票，也不该替他猜。要紧的是，提起者能不能仅凭自己的多数，就改变正在审自己案件的法院组成。停职可能有保护当事人的理由，但不能只由提起者独自决定。
问法院的路需要保持，法院不受报复地审查别人的空间也需要保持。两者并不靠一句“司法独立”自动调和，得逐处看谁能发动，谁来判断，谁能把路关掉。
还有四十三户农户的案子。他们的地被征用，补偿只有市价三分之一，说是战后另议。他们起诉补偿表，其中一位法官过去恰好替这张表写过合宪意见。申请回避，最后由他本人决定；他拒绝，理由是以前给的是一般法律意见，不涉及具体当事人。五人合议，三比二驳回，他在多数。
不能据此断定他偏心。他的理由可能有道理。问题是，关于“你能不能审这件事”的疑问，只让他自己定下来；就算他最终在少数，这个缺口也一样存在。法院属于同一个国家，并不天然不独立；独立也不能只凭法院这个名字担保。要查的是对着这张表、这个机关、这个人的实际关系。
判决之后，农户又向监察署问补偿规则和回避程序，得到的答复是：本案已经终审，不再受理。可监察署不能改判，不等于它不能问规则该不该改，不能追问那句“战后另议”准备拖到什么时候。案卷里，到第十二年，地还在用，另议还没有议。
法院解释规则，也不能借解释接过修改最高规则的全部权力。解释是否越成了改写，可以继续争论、提出新案、依程序修改未来规则；不能由法院永远独定，也不能由不服的机关自行宣布裁决作废。连“暂不解释、尚未成熟”也会让某一方的读法先作用在人身上，不能成为无限拖延的免答语。
这些安排不保证所有僵局当场化解。联合城邦的选举还是晚了一年。但后来终于举行，不会把那一年的不执行变成已经执行。缺少替代落实，是制度的一笔；拒绝发令，是相应职位的一笔。判决可以作完，人没有因此从后果里走出来。正因为如此，结案以后，有些问题才刚刚开始。
body_en: The day after the judgment, the First Executive says that the Executive Council respects the Final Court. Then comes the qualification: until the legislature formally terminates the state of war, no election order will be issued.

The court has been clear. A ceasefire is in force. For the clause postponing elections, the state of war ended when armed hostilities stopped; an election must be held by autumn. Six judges agree, five dissent. The dissenters argue that the majority has rewritten the Charter rather than interpreted it. The executive shares that view. So the majority’s binding judgment goes unimplemented.

We are back in the fictional United City-States of Ends. Its eleven-member Final Court hears Charter cases as a full bench. The Charter says its judgments bind every public body. It does not say who acts when a body refuses. The Chamber of Citizens’ term should have ended the previous winter. Its members remain in office, and the First Executive’s extended term runs with theirs.

Election commissions in the Kingdom State and South Bay State offer to prepare the vote. The council replies that member units cannot organize a national election. Nothing happens. Only the following summer, after a withdrawal agreement, does the legislature set a new date. The election finally takes place a year after the court’s deadline.

This is not simply an argument on paper. Voters have lost a year in which they should have been able to question their representatives through an election. If a final judgment becomes effective only when the losing office agrees, that office still holds the final veto.
## Final for the case, not beyond correction

Courts are not infallible. The five dissenters may have a serious argument. The majority may be wrong. But a court may be wrong does not entail that the losing public body may decline to comply. Otherwise every office could find a rival interpretation and make the judgment’s effect conditional on its own approval.

An operative judgment that must be carried out should be carried out. The executive can explain its disagreement publicly and propose changes to future rules. If it believes compliance itself would violate someone’s fundamental boundaries, it can raise that objection openly and send it into review it does not control. Until that review changes the operative decision, the decision stands. An emergency does not supply a separate power to suspend it.

This is a responsibility of office, not a philosopher’s command to an official’s conscience. A person may refuse or resign, and the system must leave room for that person’s position to be heard. But personal refusal cannot confer on the office a power to nullify the judgment. There must therefore be an alternative way to implement it, one that can be activated without the refusing body’s consent and cannot be stopped by that body.

No second army is implied. In this case the missing acts are an election order and the organization of a vote; two election commissions have offered to help. Authority and activation require concrete design. The alternative function is limited to implementing the judgment, remains reviewable, and must not become another unaccountable center. Its existence guarantees no magical success. What cannot count as an alternative is a route that still waits for the refusing office’s permission.

Conversely, mandatory compliance does not exempt the court from challenge. A case decided on the same grounds can end. New evidence or a new question can support renewed review. Judges can be held to account for bribery, abuse, or neglect. Rules can be amended for future cases. Public criticism does not require the court’s prior permission.

A last court closes a dispute, not every route toward correcting it. People need decisions they can act on now, and ways to confront mistakes afterward. Keeping one does not require surrendering the other.
## Seven judges say no

Another emergency order allows people suspected of assisting the enemy to be detained without prosecution for thirty days at a time, repeatedly. Seven judges find the provision contrary to the Charter. Four disagree. Seven is a majority—but the Fourteenth Amendment requires eight votes to invalidate an emergency order. The provision stays in force. By then 640 people have been detained under it, the longest for 150 days.

It would be inaccurate to say that the government has ignored a judgment striking down this order. No such operative judgment was made. Under the rules then in force, the court did not invalidate it. The seven judges’ objections survive as reasons, not as a decision ending the provision’s application.

Yet procedure does not settle the whole question. The threshold has changed something concrete: between a simple majority and eight votes, review that could have produced corrective action now produces reasons alone. Review still exists; one case does not establish that it has become entirely meaningless. A threshold making correction practically impossible would reduce it to a label. Here we can say something narrower and certain: seven judges’ objections did not get the detained people released.

A further detention is a further decision. New evidence, new questions, or the end of the wartime threshold can create grounds for another request. The court can decide whether a particular request is new. It cannot permanently exclude a whole class of questioners. Proposals to change the rules remain possible without retrospectively reversing a completed judgment.
## Accountability can become pressure

After the election judgment, the Chamber of Citizens impeaches the Chief Judge who wrote the majority opinion. Its stated reason is a private conversation during the court’s deliberations with the governor of South Bay, a party to the case. The conversation lasted about twenty minutes in a law school’s graduation reception room. Two teachers present say they heard no discussion of the case. The judge and governor say they talked about the ceremony and a retired judge.

The account does not let us decide whether this was misconduct. It does let us distinguish questions. A judge’s conduct can be examined. Disliking a judgment cannot by itself justify removing its author. Otherwise impeachment bypasses the requirements for reopening a case or changing future rules: no new evidence, no amendment, just a different judge. The judgment may still be evidence of bribery or abuse. What is excluded is treating an unwelcome conclusion as misconduct in itself.

Three of the four leading sponsors represented the parliamentary majority in the very case the judge decided. Those three should take no part in initiating or hearing this impeachment; proof of a private desire for revenge is not required. The conflict concerns the particular representatives, not the legislature as a whole. Disqualifying the entire body whenever it has been a party would shield judges from accountability even for bribery in those cases. Whether the charge is genuinely separable from displeasure at the judgment cannot be settled by the initiating side alone.

The impeachment also suspends the Chief Judge automatically. For three months, ten judges hear the remaining cases. The required conviction threshold is not met, and the Chief Judge returns. We cannot know how the absent judge would have voted. We can see that the initiating chamber’s majority has altered the composition of a court reviewing its actions. Suspension may have protective reasons, but it too cannot depend solely on the party initiating impeachment.

The routes for questioning judges must remain open. So must the court’s ability to review others without retaliation. The phrase judicial independence does not reconcile these needs automatically. We must ask who initiates, who decides, and who can close the route.

A separate case makes that inquiry more intimate. Forty-three farming households challenge compensation for requisitioned land, set at one third of market value, with further discussion promised only after the war. One panel judge previously advised that the very compensation schedule was constitutional. The farmers seek his recusal. Under the court’s rules he decides that application himself. He refuses, saying his earlier opinion was general, not about these particular claimants. The suit is dismissed three to two; he is in the majority.

We cannot conclude that he was biased. His explanation might be right. The structural difficulty is that the person questioned is the sole decider of whether he can hear the case. It would remain a difficulty had he been in the minority. A domestic court is not automatically dependent merely because it belongs to the same state as the defendant. Neither does the word court establish independence. The inquiry must reach the actual rule, office, and person involved.

After judgment the farmers complain to the Inspectorate about the compensation rule and recusal procedure. They are told that the case is final and will not be taken up. But an inspectorate unable to reverse the judgment can still question a rule or ask when after the war will arrive. In Year 12 the land is still in use and the promised discussion has not happened.

Interpretation likewise cannot become a second power to write the constitution. Whether a reading has crossed into amendment remains open to challenge, later cases, and lawful changes to future rules; neither the court nor its dissatisfied opponents may settle that question forever by themselves. Even declining to interpret has consequences: it lets an existing interpretation run for now. Not yet ripe cannot become a permanent refusal to answer.

These arrangements do not promise that every deadlock will be solved immediately. The UCSE’s election was still a year late. Holding it eventually does not turn that year of noncompliance into compliance. The missing alternative route is an institutional failure; refusing the order is an entry against the responsible office. A judgment may be finished while people are still living with its consequences. Some questions begin there.
